definition.text: Price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.

anchor.quote: the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price

facts.text: Demand is elastic when the absolute value of the elasticity is greater than one.

anchor.quote: Demand is described as elastic when the absolute value of the elasticity is greater than one

facts.text: Necessities tend to have inelastic demand because consumers have few substitutes.

anchor.quote: Necessities tend to have inelastic demand because consumers have few substitutes

facts.text: The availability of close substitutes is a primary determinant of elasticity.

anchor.quote: The availability of close substitutes is a primary determinant of elasticity

misconceptions.text: Students confuse the slope of the demand curve with its elasticity; slope uses absolute units while elasticity uses percentage change.
misconceptions.corrective: Elasticity compares percentage changes, so it varies along a straight-line demand curve even though the slope is constant.

examples.text: Insulin has highly inelastic demand because patients have no close substitute.

mcBank.stem: A 10 percent price increase reduces quantity demanded by 25 percent. This demand is best described as
options: elastic
unit elastic
inelastic
perfectly inelastic

mapping.marginal benefit: the change in quantity demanded from the next price step
mapping.marginal cost: the revenue change from that price step

definition.text: A demand curve shows the quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to purchase at each price, holding other factors constant.

anchor.quote: the quantity of a good that consumers are willing and able to purchase at each price, holding all other factors constant

facts.text: Demand curves typically slope downward, reflecting the law of demand.

anchor.quote: Demand curves typically slope downward, reflecting the law of demand

facts.text: A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve, while a change in income or tastes shifts the curve.

anchor.quote: A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve

misconceptions.text: Students treat a price change as shifting the demand curve, when it only causes movement along the curve.

examples.text: When coffee prices fall, consumers buy more coffee, moving down the demand curve.

mcBank.stem: A decrease in consumer income for a normal good will most directly
options: shift the demand curve leftward
move quantity demanded up along the curve
make demand perfectly elastic
raise the equilibrium price

definition.text: Market equilibrium occurs at the price where the quantity demanded by buyers equals the quantity supplied by sellers.

anchor.quote: the price where the quantity demanded by buyers equals the quantity supplied by sellers

facts.text: At the equilibrium price the opposing pressures of demand and supply are balanced and the price has no tendency to change.

anchor.quote: the opposing pressures of demand and supply are balanced and there is no tendency for the price to change

facts.text: A price above equilibrium creates a surplus that pushes it down; a price below creates a shortage that pushes it up.

anchor.quote: a surplus pushes it down, and when the price is below equilibrium a shortage pushes it up

misconceptions.text: Students think market equilibrium means nothing changes, when buying and selling continue and only the price is stable.
misconceptions.corrective: Equilibrium is a balance of ongoing opposing pressures, not a frozen market.

examples.text: If a price ceiling holds the price below equilibrium, the resulting shortage persists because the restoring rise is blocked.

mcBank.stem: At a price above the market equilibrium price, what happens?
options: A surplus forms and pushes the price down toward equilibrium
A shortage forms and pushes the price up
Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
The equilibrium price rises permanently

mapping.perturbation: a price set above or below equilibrium
mapping.restoring force: the surplus or shortage that pushes the price back to balance

definition.text: A wage-price spiral is a self-reinforcing cycle in which rising prices lead workers to demand higher wages, and higher wage costs lead firms to raise prices further.

anchor.quote: rising prices lead workers to demand higher wages, and the higher wage costs lead firms to raise prices further

facts.text: The wage-price spiral is positive feedback: an initial change is amplified rather than damped.

anchor.quote: positive feedback, in which an initial change is amplified rather than damped

facts.text: Unlike negative feedback, positive feedback drives the system further from where it started.

anchor.quote: positive feedback drives the system further from where it started

misconceptions.text: Students assume positive feedback is beneficial, when it names amplification regardless of whether the outcome is good.
misconceptions.corrective: Positive feedback describes runaway amplification, which is often harmful, as in an inflation spiral.

examples.text: Expectations of continued inflation can lock in a wage-price spiral until policy interrupts the loop.

mcBank.stem: A wage-price spiral is best classified as which kind of feedback?
options: Positive feedback that amplifies the initial change
Negative feedback that damps the initial change
A one-time shock with no feedback
An external constraint on the market

mapping.feedback path: workers demanding higher wages that raise firms' costs
mapping.effect on input: further price increases that amplify the cycle

definition.text: Consumer choice theory models how a consumer maximizes utility subject to a budget constraint.

anchor.quote: how a consumer maximizes utility subject to a budget constraint

facts.text: The consumer selects the affordable bundle of goods that yields the highest satisfaction.

anchor.quote: selects the affordable bundle of goods that yields the highest satisfaction

facts.text: At the optimal choice, utility cannot be increased without exceeding the budget, so the consumer faces a tradeoff between goods.

anchor.quote: utility cannot be increased without exceeding the budget, so the consumer faces a tradeoff between goods

misconceptions.text: Students propose the bundle a consumer would most like, ignoring that the budget constraint makes most bundles infeasible.
misconceptions.corrective: The optimal bundle is the best one the consumer can actually afford, not the most desirable one.

examples.text: With a fixed budget, buying more concert tickets means buying fewer meals out.

mcBank.stem: In consumer choice theory, the optimal bundle is the one that
options: maximizes utility within the budget
ignores the budget entirely
costs the most money
contains every available good

mapping.decision variables: the bundle of goods the consumer chooses
mapping.tradeoff: choosing more of one good means affording less of another

definition.text: An economic model is a simplified representation of reality that keeps the features relevant to a question and discards the rest.

anchor.quote: a simplified representation of reality that keeps the features relevant to a question and discards the rest

facts.text: Models such as supply and demand make assumptions, like rational choice or perfect competition, that do not hold exactly.

anchor.quote: make assumptions, like rational choice or perfect competition, that do not hold exactly

facts.text: A model is useful when its assumptions are close enough for the question at hand, and misleading when a key assumption breaks.

anchor.quote: useful when its assumptions are close enough for the question at hand, and misleading when a key assumption breaks

misconceptions.text: Students treat an economic model as literally true and apply it where its assumptions clearly fail.
misconceptions.corrective: A model is a tool whose conclusions hold only while its assumptions approximately hold.

examples.text: Perfect-competition predictions mislead in a market dominated by one firm.

mcBank.stem: An economic model is most useful when
options: its assumptions hold closely enough
it includes every real detail
it makes no assumptions at all
it predicts the future perfectly

mapping.model: an economic model such as supply and demand
mapping.kept features: the features relevant to the question
mapping.discarded features: the real-world details the model discards
mapping.breaking assumption: assumptions like rational choice or perfect competition

definition.text: A natural experiment uses a policy change or external event affecting one group but not another to estimate a causal effect from observational data.

anchor.quote: a policy change or external event that affects one group but not another to estimate a causal effect from observational data

facts.text: The causal claim is credible only if the two groups were comparable apart from the change.

anchor.quote: whether the two groups were comparable apart from the change

facts.text: The effect can be attributed to the policy rather than to a confounding factor only when that comparability holds.

anchor.quote: the difference can be attributed to the policy rather than to a confounding factor

misconceptions.text: Students accept a natural-experiment result as causal without checking whether the compared groups were otherwise alike.
misconceptions.corrective: The causal claim holds only if the groups differ just in the policy, not in confounders.

examples.text: A minimum-wage change in one state but not its neighbor lets economists estimate the employment effect.

mapping.association: the difference in outcomes between the affected and unaffected groups
mapping.proposed cause: the policy change or external event
mapping.alternative explanation: a confounding factor that also differs between the groups

definition.text: In the circular flow of income, money that households earn returns to firms as spending unless it leaks out of the flow as saving, taxes, or spending on imports.

anchor.quote: money that households earn returns to firms as spending unless it leaks out of the flow as saving, taxes, or spending on imports

facts.text: Leakages are balanced by injections such as investment, government spending, and exports that add spending back into the flow.

anchor.quote: Leakages are balanced by injections such as investment, government spending, and exports that add spending back into the flow

facts.text: When total leakages equal total injections, the circular flow is in balance and national income neither rises nor falls.

anchor.quote: When total leakages equal total injections, the circular flow is in balance and national income neither rises nor falls

misconceptions.text: Students treat saving as money that disappears from the economy rather than a leakage that must be matched by an injection.
misconceptions.corrective: Saving is not destroyed; in balance it re-enters the flow as investment, government spending, or exports.

examples.text: Household saving deposited in a bank is lent to firms as investment, re-injecting money that had leaked out of the flow.

mcBank.stem: For the circular flow of income to be in balance, total leakages must equal
options: total injections
total consumption
the money supply
the trade deficit

mapping.system: the economy’s circular flow of income
mapping.inputs: injections such as investment, government spending, and exports
mapping.outputs: leakages such as saving, taxes, and imports

definition.text: The capital stock is the total quantity of equipment, structures, and tools available for production; it rises through gross investment and falls through depreciation.

anchor.quote: rises through gross investment and falls through depreciation

facts.text: Net investment, which is gross investment minus depreciation, is the change in the capital stock over a period.

anchor.quote: gross investment minus depreciation, is the change in the capital stock over a period

facts.text: The capital stock grows only when net investment is positive.

anchor.quote: the stock grows only when net investment is positive

misconceptions.text: Students expect the capital stock to jump when investment rises, confusing the level (the stock of capital) with the flow (investment per year).
misconceptions.corrective: Higher investment raises the stock gradually over time; the stock does not jump when the flow changes.

examples.text: A factory's machinery builds up over years of net investment; one year of higher spending nudges the trajectory, it does not double the stock overnight.

mcBank.stem: The capital stock grows over time only when
options: gross investment exceeds depreciation in that period
interest rates fall to historically low levels
the labor force participation rate increases
consumer spending rises faster than saving does

mapping.level: the quantity of capital available for production

definition.text: A proxy variable is an observable stand-in used to measure a construct that cannot be observed directly.

anchor.quote: an observable stand-in, to measure a construct they cannot observe directly

facts.text: GDP is used as a proxy for economic well-being, but it captures only marketed output and misses unpaid work, income distribution, and environmental costs.

anchor.quote: it captures only marketed output and misses unpaid work, income distribution, and environmental costs

facts.text: Because the proxy is not the construct, conclusions drawn from it inherit whatever the measure leaves out.

anchor.quote: Because the proxy is not the construct, conclusions drawn from it inherit whatever the measure leaves out

misconceptions.text: Students treat GDP as if it were well-being itself, forgetting it is only a proxy that misses unpaid work and distribution.
misconceptions.corrective: Hold the construct (well-being) fixed and ask what a different measure would capture that GDP does not.

examples.text: Two countries with equal GDP can differ sharply in well-being if one has far more unpaid care work and a more equal income distribution.

mcBank.stem: GDP is used as a proxy for economic well-being, but it
options: misses unpaid work, distribution, and environmental costs
cannot be computed without a full national census every year
is rejected by most national statistics offices
is identical to a nation's total population

mapping.what it misses: unpaid work, income distribution, and environmental costs

definition.text: People who have given up looking for work are classified as out of the labor force, not unemployed.

anchor.quote: people who have given up looking are classified as out of the labor force, not unemployed

facts.text: Discouraged workers who are excluded make unemployment look lower than the felt experience of joblessness.

anchor.quote: discouraged workers who are excluded make unemployment look lower than the felt experience of joblessness

facts.text: Where this boundary is drawn changes the measured unemployment rate.

anchor.quote: Where this boundary is drawn changes the measured unemployment rate

misconceptions.text: Students read the unemployment rate as a neutral fact, missing that the labor-force boundary excludes discouraged workers by choice.
misconceptions.corrective: Recount the rate including discouraged workers and ask whose situation each definition makes visible.

examples.text: In a weak job market the official rate can fall simply because discouraged workers stop looking and drop out of the labor force.

mcBank.stem: A discouraged worker who has stopped looking for a job is
options: classified as out of the labor force, not unemployed
still counted as unemployed in the official statistics
automatically guaranteed a government job placement
the largest single category in every modern economy

mapping.stake of the boundary: the measured unemployment rate and the policy it drives

definition.text: The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the next best alternative that must be given up.

anchor.quote: the opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the next best alternative that must be given up

facts.text: A decision that looks free still has an opportunity cost if it uses time or resources that could have produced something else.

anchor.quote: A decision that looks free still has an opportunity cost if it uses time or resources that could have produced something else

facts.text: Rational decision-makers weigh the opportunity cost, not just the out-of-pocket price.

anchor.quote: Rational decision-makers weigh the opportunity cost, not just the out-of-pocket price

misconceptions.text: Students count only the money paid and ignore the value of the foregone alternative.
misconceptions.corrective: Always ask what the next best use of the time or money was; that foregone value is the real cost.

examples.text: A free concert ticket still costs the wage and study time you give up to attend — its opportunity cost is not zero.

mcBank.stem: The opportunity cost of a choice is
options: the value of the next best alternative given up
only the money paid out of pocket for it
the combined value of every option not chosen
zero whenever the choice happens to feel free

definition.text: By the law of supply, a higher price raises the quantity producers are willing to supply, so the supply curve slopes upward.

anchor.quote: a higher price raises the quantity that producers are willing to supply, so the supply curve slopes upward

facts.text: A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve, while a change in input costs or technology shifts the whole curve.

anchor.quote: A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve, while a change in input costs or technology shifts the whole curve

facts.text: Quantity supplied is a flow per period, not a fixed stock.

anchor.quote: Quantity supplied is a flow per period, not a fixed stock

misconceptions.text: Students treat a price change as shifting the whole supply curve, confusing a move along the curve with a shift of it.
misconceptions.corrective: A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; only non-price factors shift the curve.

examples.text: When the price of coffee rises, growers offer more beans (move along the curve); a frost that kills plants shifts the curve instead.

mcBank.stem: Along the curve, a rise in a good's own price
options: increases the quantity supplied
shifts the entire curve to the left
always lowers the firm’s input costs
has no effect on the quantity offered

definition.text: A producer has a comparative advantage in the good it can make at the lower opportunity cost, even if another producer is better at making everything.

anchor.quote: A producer has a comparative advantage in the good it can make at the lower opportunity cost

facts.text: When each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades, total output rises and both can consume beyond what they could produce alone.

anchor.quote: When each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades, total output rises

facts.text: Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost, not from absolute skill.

anchor.quote: Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost, not from absolute skill

misconceptions.text: Students think the producer who is best at everything (absolute advantage) should make everything, missing comparative advantage.
misconceptions.corrective: Compare opportunity costs, not absolute skill; specialize where your opportunity cost is lowest.

examples.text: A lawyer who types faster than her assistant still gains by letting the assistant type, freeing her higher-value legal hours.

mcBank.stem: A country should specialize in the good for which it has
options: the lower opportunity cost
the largest total workforce
an absolute advantage in everything
the highest selling price abroad

definition.text: An externality is a cost or benefit from a transaction that falls on a third party who is not part of the exchange.

anchor.quote: An externality is a cost or benefit from a transaction that falls on a third party who is not part of the exchange

facts.text: With a negative externality like pollution, the market produces more than the socially efficient quantity because the price excludes the spillover cost.

anchor.quote: the market produces more than the socially efficient quantity because the price excludes the spillover cost

facts.text: Correcting an externality means making decision-makers face the costs or benefits the market boundary leaves out.

anchor.quote: making the decision-makers face the costs or benefits the market boundary leaves out

misconceptions.text: Students assume a free market always reaches the efficient quantity, ignoring costs that fall outside the price.
misconceptions.corrective: Ask who else is affected by the transaction; a cost outside the price means the market over-produces.

examples.text: A factory that dumps waste into a river imposes a cost on downstream users that its product price never reflects.

mcBank.stem: A negative externality such as pollution leads a free market to
options: produce more than the socially efficient quantity
produce exactly the efficient quantity anyway
shut the polluting industry down on its own
set a price that already includes every spillover

mapping.system: the market transaction between buyer and seller
mapping.boundary: the price that coordinates the exchange
mapping.what crosses: the costs and benefits captured in the price
mapping.what is excluded: spillover costs or benefits that fall on third parties

definition.text: A monopoly is a market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry.

anchor.quote: a market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry

facts.text: Unlike a price-taking competitive firm, a monopoly is a price maker: it can raise price by restricting the quantity it sells.

anchor.quote: a monopoly is a price maker: it can raise price by restricting the quantity it sells

facts.text: Because it produces less and charges more than a competitive market, a monopoly creates deadweight loss.

anchor.quote: a monopoly creates deadweight loss

misconceptions.text: Students think a monopoly can charge any price it likes with no limit, ignoring that higher prices cut the quantity sold.
misconceptions.corrective: A monopoly is constrained by the demand curve: to raise price it must sell less.

examples.text: A patent-protected drug with no substitute lets its maker set a high price by limiting supply, until the patent expires.

mcBank.stem: Unlike a competitive firm, a monopoly can
options: raise its price by restricting quantity
sell all it wants at the going market price
be forced to take the market price as given
never earn more than zero economic profit
